<reason>Both sides argued competently, but B built and sustained the more damaging line of clash. B's distinction between suffering (correctable until death) and death (permanently uncorrectable) was never squarely defeated by A's "harm cuts both ways" reply, which conflated two different kinds of irreversibility. More decisively, when A proposed "constitutional entrenchment" of eligibility criteria as a safeguard against drift, B turned this into a direct liability by pointing out that Canada's courts expanded MAID using exactly the autonomy/equality reasoning A's whole case rests on, and that Canada's original law already had a diagnosis/foreseeability-style line that fell to that reasoning. A's closing never actually answered this specific point—it simply reasserted that the motion's line is diagnosis-based without explaining why that line would resist the same principled erosion. B also cleanly separated palliative sedation (side effect) from assisted dying (aim), defusing A's attempt to force symmetry in "trusting doctors." A's best material—leveraging B's concession that some suffering may remain unrelieved, and the "don't strip choice to fix coerced choice" line—was rhetorically strong and kept the debate close, but it didn't resolve the coherence problem in A's core safeguard proposal that B had exposed and pressed through rebuttal 2 and closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's rebuttal 2 turning A's proposed "constitutional entrenchment" safeguard into direct evidence for the slippery slope (Canada's courts used the same autonomy logic to strike a diagnosis-based limit), reinforced unanswered in B's closing.</best_rebuttal>
